1: multa: the neuter plural adjective functions substantively as the accusative direct object. diuque: although the conjunction may seem unnecessary, it emphasizes the multiple burdens the speaker has endured. uitiis = “by faults” (OLD s.v. uitium 3b)
2: pectore: the ablative following cede can convey a sense of movement away or separation (OLD s.v. cedo 2-4), even without a preposition. turpis: the speaker’s negative feelings toward love are explicit.
3: adserui iam me: the speaker frames love as enslavement and asserts his own agency in escaping (OLD s.v. assero 3).
4: puduit ferre, tulisse pudet: the shifting tenses emphasize the speaker’s sense of regret.
5: uicimus: the perfect tense suggests the completed aspect of the speaker’s victory. The imagery is reminiscent of statuary where a representation of a subjugated population is trod upon by a victor. The equestrian statue of Marcus Aurelius (once believed to be of Constantine) in Rome’s Capitoline Museum is described in a medieval text (Mirabilia Urbis Romae, sect. 16) as depicting a statue of a bound king beneath the horse’s raised forehoof.
6: cornua: the speaker’s new-found horns are a source of strength or pride (OLD s.v. cornu 1d).
7: perfer et obdura: the speaker’s peptalk nearly quotes a verse by Catullus (c. 8.11: sed obstinata mente perfer, obdura). The speaker in Catullus’s poem also attempts to convince himself to assert his independence from a puella. olim: this adverb can refer to the past or the future (OLD s.v. olim 1 vs. 3). The future perfect proderit encourages interpreting it as referring to the future here.
8: The sentiment echoes elements of the description of the honeyed cup in Lucretius (DRN 1.936-50) wherein bitter medicine conveys important medical benefit. lassis = “to weary ones.” The substantive adjective lends the verse much of its gnomic force.
9: In the next four couplets, the speaker recalls—with some incredulity—what he has suffered in the name of love. The dominant scenario is that of an exclusus amator, or “locked-out lover,” which Ovid elsewhere pairs with a paraclausithyron, or a song sung outside a closed door. The speaker here does not mention any poetic production pursued while he was locked out, but he does pair this scenario with another elegiac trope—seruitium amoris or “the servitude of love”—in verses 10-11 (#Link to other discussions.) ergo ego: the near echo between these words is redoubled by their repetition at the beginning of the next couplet. The force falls on ego, as if the speaker is saying, “Did I really…?”
10: ingenuum: the speaker notes the free-born status of his body, anticipating his mention of servitude (seruus) in verse 11. dura: scansion shows this to be ablative in agreement with humo.
11: nescio cui = “for I-don’t-know-who.” The dative of reference could here be regarded as a “dative of advantage” to specify the beneficiary of the speaker’s action (A&G 376). The juxtaposition of nescio cui and ego emphasizes the speaker’s disbelief that he so debased himself for an unknown rival. It also bears hints of an accusation of promiscuity on the part of the puella.
12: ut = “as” with an implied indicative verb. A rendering of the verse in English word order might yield the following: excubui ut seruus (excubit) ante clausam domum. P and Y both read et, although a second scribe writing in darker ink in Y suggests ut.
13: uidi: the direct object is not stated but implied in the cum clause (which, despite the punctuation in LL, continues through 14).
14: inualidum: when modifying latus, the sense is “weak” due to sexual exhaustion. For the sexual sense of latus, see the Grammar Commentary for 3.7.36. referens: the nominative participle modifies amator in 13. emeritum: similar to inualidum, the implication is of something “worn out” through sexual effort.
15: hoc: refers to what was just described in verses 13 and 14. quod: introduces a substantive clause with an indicative verb. Translate as “the fact that” (A&G 575).
16: hostibus: the sense of this verse is that the speaker would only wish the embarrassment he felt on his enemies.
17: lateri: dative with adhaesi (OLD s.v. adhaereo 5b), but the fact that it naturally follows fixus emphasizes the meaning. The sexual overtones latus carries in 14 are downplayed to emphasize a different degree of devotion.
18:
The speaker claims roles beyond an amatory one.
Manuscript Y includes some punctuation to set off the different noun groupings.
19: per me comitata = “accompanied by me.” Cf. Amores 3.12 for the speaker’s insistence upon his role in shaping Corinna’s reputation.
20: multis: dative of reference (A&G 376) with hints of possession. amoris: read with causa.
21: In 21-24 the speaker poses two rhetorical questions featuring preterition. The first couplet distills a central theme of Amores 3.3, namely, the idea that the speaker’s puella can lie without negative consequence to her. turpia: the placement of this word first in the verse stresses the speaker’s appraisal of the puella’s mendacia. quid referam: “Why would I recount…?” uanae = “false” (OLD s.v. uanus 3)
22: in mea damna: “to my punishment.” Cf. Amores 3.3.13-16 for how a woman’s false oaths could precipitate her lover’s punishment rather than her own.
23: quid: resupply referam from 21. Cf. Amores 1.4.17-20 for signals and notes exchanged at a dinner party.
25: dicta erat: the speaker shifts to third-person narration (after, e.g., placebas in 19). The implied subject ea can be inferred from the feminine singular form of dicta. Supplying an infinitive esse after dicta erat may ease English translation. praeceps amensque: the caesura after mihi clarifies that these nominatives describe the subject of cucurri (rather than dicta erat). Modern editors sometimes place an emdash after mihi to clarify sense.
26: ueni: with simple aspect, the verb can be understood as saying, “I arrived.” riuali: another dative of reference (A&G 376) with a sense of “advantage” (cf. nescio cui, 11).
27: his…ferendis: one can render this gerundive phrase into English with an ablative gerund taking a direct object. In this verse, the object is expressed by his and et quae taceo (e.g., “By enduring these things and things which I’m silent about…”). et quae taceo: the speaker claims he is leaving some of his lover’s grievances unsaid. duraui: the main verb. saepe: read with ferendis.
28: quaere: a return to the second person, now an imperative. Does the speaker address the puella or Love (as in verse 2)? qui: the relative clause of characteristic (A&G 535) only makes sense when the antecedent is identified as alium rather than me. ista: the demonstrative gestures back—with attendant distaste—to his in 27.
29: The speaker likens the end of his amatory journey to a ship arriving safely in port. See Vergil’s Georgics 1.303-4 for the practice of wreathing ship sterns with flowers at the conclusion of a voyage. iam: as in verse 3, the speaker presents his escape from love’s perils as already accomplished. Scansion shows mea and redimita to be nominative, uotiua and corona to be ablative. Note the graphic word order, with the word puppis surrounded by the votive wreath.
30: lenta: because the speaker’s “amatory ship” is safely moored, it can be “unconcerned” (OLD s.v. lentus 9) about the motion of the surrounding waters.
31: The speaker directly addresses the puella again. desine: the imperative’s complementary infinitive is postponed to the beginning of the next verse. A fourth-foot caesura provides editors reason to place a comma between uerba and potentia. The portion of the verse after the comma explains how the woman’s uerba have changed.
32: sum is implied after ego. The compression and balance (nunc…ante) of the final sentence lend this verse a sense of finality.
33: lunctantur: the subjects are postponed to the next verse. in contraria = “in opposite directions” (OLD s.v. contrarius 1) tendunt: the verbs at either end of this verse (with the obect pectus leue in the middle) visually enact the tug-o’-war the speaker is describing.
34: hac: the adverb means “this way” or “in this direction” (OLD s.v. hac 1). uincit amor: the speaker alludes to a verse from Vergil’s Eclogues 10: omnia uincit amor, et nos cedamus Amori (“Love conquers all; let us, too, yield to love”).
35: odero: for this defective verb, a perfect form has the force of the present and the future perfect has the sense of the future (A&G 205b). si non: potero can be resupplied as the main verb in this protasis. inuitus = “unwillingly”
36: With an analogy drawn from animal husbandry, the speaker casually equates “not loving” with “hating” while also suggesting a sense of resignation to one’s circumstances. quae: the antecedent appears in the previous clause. The subject of odit and habet is also drawn from the first clause in the verse. Manuscript Y initially reads hodit for odit, but a second hand has marked the h with a punctum delens. The verse in Manuscript P shows signs of damage, but odit is clearly legible at the end of the verse.
37: The couplet more specifically illustrates the opposite directions (see 33-34) in which the speaker feels pulled by his feelings. At the same time, the couplet lacks pronouns and possessive adjectives, as if the speaker is reflecting broadly on his personal tendencies—and not thinking of a specific lover when admitting to his fixation on physical attributes. nequitiam: the speaker does not claim to flee his puella but a negative quality apparent in his puella’s behavior. fugientem: the participle functions substantively. Because of the first-person subject of fugio, one can infer me is the pronoun described by this participle. forma: as with nequitiam at the beginning of the verse, the speaker differentiates the puella from some of her specific physical and behavioral attributes. Manuscripts P and Y read reduc& (future tense), but a second hand in Y has proposed reducit.
38: The two parts of the pentameter verse reiterate the halves of the previous hexameter, but there is also a syntactical parallelism between the beginning of the hexameter (nequitiam fugio) and the end of the pentameter (corpus amo).
39: ego nec sine te…tecum: as if correcting for the general sense of the previous couplet, the speaker addresses the puella directly and emphatically specifies that he is thinking of her.
41: fores = esses, an optative subjunctive indicating an unaccomplished wish in the present (A&G 441). For forms of uolo taking the subjunctive without ut, see A&G 565. uellem: a potential subjunctive (i.e., “I would have wanted either that…”; cf. the note to A&G 447.1).
42: non facit ad: an idiomatic expression meaning “does not work with” or “does not suit” (OLD s.v. facio 30). mores…forma: the opposing concepts of verses 37 (forma) and 38 (morum) return. tam: word order means the adverb reads most naturally with bona, but its force may still linger when a reader reaches malos at the verse’s end.
43: The tension between behavior and appearance continues to preoccupy the speaker.
44: “Wretched me! She is stronger in her flaws.” me miserum: accusative of exclamation (A&G 397d). uitiis…suis: ablative of respect (rather than comparison, for which ualeo more often uses quam). illa: when interpreted as referring to the puella instead of her facies (43), the possessive suis would refer to the puella’s moral flaws rather than flaws in her appearance (which seems flawless).
45: parce: without a stated object, the sense is “be merciful” (OLD s.v. parco 3). The speaker resumes his address of the puella. per: “by” or “for the sake of.” The preposition repeated in this verse and the next three verses designates the reasons for which the speaker begs the puella’s mercy. o: the exclamation postponed after the preposition communicates the speaker’s passion. The reading o is not attested in Manuscript P or Y; P is barely legible, and a second hand in darker ink in Y has written cor in the space between p and lecti, obscuring the original letters (although per and o would appear to fit). socialia iura: the speaker’s language suggests a quasi-legal, formal relationship, albeit one formalized in bed. omnis: modifying deos at the end of 46 (after the intervening relative clause).
46: The enjambment from the previous verse allows the passionate tone of 45 to continue, while the speaker presents the gods as willing participants in the puella’s false oaths. A rendering of the prepositional phrase (beginning in 45) in English word order might yield per omnis deos qui saepe dant se tibi fallendos. fallendos: after verbs of giving (dant), a gerundive in agreement with an object (se) expresses purpose (A&G 500.4).
47: faciem: the speaker recalls what he regards as the puella’s chief asset from 43. mihi: dative of reference with instar (A&G 376).
49: selige: a correcting scribe in Y was active in proposing ius elige tantum (as well as quicquid for quidquid earlier in the verse). Reading tantum as an adverb and retaining tu (such that selige has no stated object) better tees up the alternative indirect questions of 50.
50: uelis: “whether you want.” The interrogative particle is omitted from the first indirect question (A&G 335a). anne: introduces the second of the two indirect questions. amem: the speaker lends the second indirect question deliberative force (“or should I love…”), thus eschewing syntactical parallelism between the alternative questions.
51: lintea: as with uela, the idiom with dare is “to spread sail” or otherwise open one’s sails to the wind. (OLD s.v. uelum 2) dem…utar: the difference between potential and hortatory subjunctives with first-person present verbs feels insignificant. “I would rather spread sails” and “Let me rather spread sails” both communicate the speaker’s preference to retain a sense of agency in what he feels. ferentibus = secundis (“favorable” OLD s.v. secundus A1)
52: A syntactically complicated final verse that lays bare the speaker’s ongoing struggle with his conflicting feelings. A rendering of the purpose clause in English word order might yield ut uelim amare [eam] quam, si nolim, cogar amare, but the flexibility of Latin word order permits the speaker to place his desire to want to love in the emphatic final position. ut, quam: these same words in reverse order often appear after potius (e.g., “I would rather A than that B occur…”, but this ut introduces a purpose clause, while quam introduces a relative clause with eam as an implied antecedent. nolim: present subjunctive in the protasis of a future less vivid conditional. cogar: present subjunctive in the apodosis of future less vivid conditional nested within a relative clause. amare: a complementary infinitive with cogar that is reused to complete the sense of uelim. uelim: present subjunctive in a purpose clause.
